title: Is Written Feedback a Waste of Time?
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick reads a Contemporary Educational Psychology study of 937 German secondary students to ask an uncomfortable question about marking: if a fifth of students ignore written feedback outright and almost half of those who act on it get no better, what exactly is the return on the hours teachers spend? He pulls out the counterintuitive findings — higher-performing students were less likely to improve, students who said feedback was useful still failed to act on it, boys disengaged more than girls even after controlling for ability and motivation, and detailed feedback with specific examples improved implementation though not initial engagement. He sets this alongside Dylan Wiliam's estimate that England spends roughly £2.5bn a year on feedback for almost no measurable gain, and Kluger and DeNisi's finding that 38% of feedback interventions actually made performance worse. The essay is careful not to conclude that marking is worthless: Hendrick defends reading student work for its diagnostic and relational value, the 'formative dividend' of spotting patterns and misconceptions. His actual target is ritual — marking done because it is expected rather than because it works. He closes on a hybrid future in which comparative judgement plus AI transcription of brief audio comments handles the mechanical load, freeing teachers for the high-impact work of discussing and modelling revision. A strong candidate for any workload or assessment policy review.
points: The headline statistic worth carrying into a department meeting: roughly two-thirds of students either ignored the feedback entirely or revised without improving.
The gender gap in feedback disengagement survived controls for cognitive ability, motivation and prior attainment, pointing at socialisation rather than capability.
Hendrick separates marking's feedback function from its diagnostic function, and it is the second — seeing patterns and misconceptions across a class — that he thinks justifies the time.
Kluger and DeNisi's finding that 38% of feedback interventions depressed performance is the counterweight to any blanket 'feedback is good practice' claim.
The proposed replacement is concrete: comparative judgement plus short audio comments synthesised by AI, with the teacher kept in the loop rather than automated out of it.
quotes: A recent study published in Contemporary Educational Psychology reveals some uncomfortable truths about how secondary school students actually engage with the feedback they receive. Researchers examined 937 German students who were given feedback on their English writing tasks and asked to revise their work.

So in total, that means about two-thirds of students either ignored feedback entirely or failed to benefit from it despite making revisions. This raises serious questions about the efficiency of marking books with written feedback.

Perhaps most surprising is that higher-performing students were actually less likely to improve after receiving feedback. This counterintuitive result suggests that there’s either a motivation issue where these students may feel less compelled to make substantive changes, or there is some kind of ceiling effect of diminishing returns where further improvement becomes increasingly difficult.

Firstly, male students were significantly more likely than female students to ignore feedback completely. This gender gap persisted even after controlling for cognitive abilities, motivation, and prior performance, suggesting deeper socialization factors at play. The researchers noted that this aligns with previous findings showing male students tend to approach evaluative situations more competitively and may be more likely to dismiss external input.

Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis found that while feedback interventions overall had a modest positive effect on performance, 38% of the feedback interventions actually decreased performance. This startling finding challenges our fundamental assumptions about feedback's universally beneficial nature.

The issue isn't that feedback cannot be effective, but rather that traditional approaches to marking are done not because they’re effective, but because we think we should do it. Without addressing the mechanisms of student disengagement, from gender differences in feedback receptivity to the gap between recognising feedback value and knowing how to implement it, many educators may be unknowingly performing a laborious, time-intensive ritual that serves institutional expectations rather than actual student learning.

Personally I don’t think marking is a total waste of time (as much as I hated it), indeed there are strong reasons for teachers to engage with student work beyond simply providing feedback. Carefully reading a student's work demonstrates respect for their efforts and helps teachers gain deeper insights into their thinking, misconceptions, and progress.
